extracted.intended_audience: marketing and advertising researchers; grantmakers and program evaluators
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting methodological and evaluative criteria for designing, measuring, and interpreting research on advertising effects and consumer behavior (panel, experimental, accounting, psychometric, and organizational-context considerations). Useful for reviewers/funders judging quality of such studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of study environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately choose study environment to control complexity (example: small-city environment chosen to avoid added complexity of family decision-making in major urban areas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sampling locales that reduce confounding complexity for exploratory studies; expand to larger/complex settings (e.g., Chicago) only after feasibility and control issues are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of longitudinal consumer panel design
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ panel designs (e.g., couples interviewed five times) to collect a wide range of information about the purchase decision process and to test complex decision models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel studies allow modification/addition of measures during the study, support test-development methodology, and permit more intensive exploration of influences over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure sensitivity for advertising exposure and attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure measuring instruments are sufficiently sensitive; simple measures (e.g., whether advertisements had been noted) may be relatively insensitive and mask relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid near-universal binary awareness measures when variation is required; refine exposure metrics and attitude instruments; add or modify measures during panel studies to improve sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ranking of assets as indicant of attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Rank assets by respondents in terms of a relative preference criterion; interpret this ranking as an indicant of attitude toward the assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preference-ranking measures when appropriate to infer attitudes influencing asset-accumulation decisions; validate that rankings correspond to attitudinal constructs of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multiple potential influences as covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate other possible influences such as income, education, expected wealth, personality characteristics, and long-run goals when testing advertising effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these variables as control or explanatory covariates in models of asset accumulation, consumption, or other buyer behavior to isolate advertising effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper accounting for intangible assets when measuring firm returns
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating the relationship between advertising expenditure and firm rates of return, include intangible assets (such as advertising and R&D) in firm book value and correct current advertising outlays to include provision for amortizing advertising capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to include intangibles or to amortize advertising capital can create an apparent positive relationship between advertising level and measured rates of return; use improved asset estimation methods to avoid biased inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate rates of amortization of advertising expenditures by industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate annual rates of amortization for advertising capital (industry examples: beer 40–50% per annum; cigarettes 33–40% per annum) to measure the value of intangible advertising assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use industry-specific amortization estimates to convert current ad outlays into comparable capital values; unreliable estimates (e.g., in some industries) should be acknowledged and sensitivity-tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptualize advertising as an intangible service / joint product
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat advertising as an intangible service provided to consumers and as a joint product supplementary to physical output, which affects analyses of competition and market performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptualization can change competitive implications; analysis should consider advertising as creating a commodity-like service and incorporate it into demand and competition models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link unobservable mental processes to observable phenomena through theory and testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because information handling (and many internal states) are not directly observable, develop theories that link unobservable mental processes to observable outcomes, and test hypotheses derived from those theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If observed phenomena occur as predicted by theory-derived hypotheses, confidence in the unobservable-process descriptions increases; emphasize theoretical development coupled with empirical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research information handling as acquisition, processing, and utilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame information handling into three components: acquisition (sensing, attending, comprehending, cue selection), processing (sorting, scaling, computing, evaluating, storing), and utilization (memory, retrievability, effect on beliefs and behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measures and methods tailored to each component; recognize that processing is hardest to measure and may require indirect tests linking to observable behavior and attitude formation/change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and validate psychographic/lifestyle measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Design psychographic scales to measure activities, interests, and opinions (life-style), determine latent dimensions, and compare predictive validity with less comprehensive measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test scale structure (latent dimensions) and predictive power for product/person perception and usage; validate against alternative instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predict media choice using choice models with syndicated data
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop media-choice models (e.g., TV program choice) that can predict individual choice using relatively inexpensive syndicated viewing data rather than detailed individual inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model should be testable, extendable (e.g., segmentation, preferred mix prediction), and applicable for advertiser selection of program alternatives similar to target preferences; refine mathematical assumptions as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and quantify causal pathways from advertising stimuli to behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify and empirically test hypothesized causal chains (for example: advertising stimulus → memory of content → brand comprehension → confidence in judging brand → intention to buy → purchase behavior) and estimate relative strengths of each influence using panel data and mathematical (computer-solved) equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal/panel data and structural-equation–type approaches to estimate pathways; report effect sizes and strengths for each link; update theoretical structure with new empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precisely define stimuli and conduct content analysis of advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Define advertising stimuli precisely in terms of their content; analyze advertisements in terms of attitudinal, comprehension, and intention components to attribute observed effects correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without precise stimulus definition, attributing observed effects to ads vs other stimuli is impossible; include content-coding methodologies and link content dimensions to outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments for replication, control, speed, and low cost (computer-controlled experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computer-controlled experimental techniques to enable experimenters with minimal technical skills to design sophisticated communications experiments quickly; allow rapid administration, storage, statistical analysis, and exact replication across geographies and population segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage computerized administration to improve experimental control and reduce time/cost; verify stability across replications and consistency with traditional methods before generalizing to field settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance realism and experimental control
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the appropriate level of stimulus realism: the technique can present simple well-defined stimuli for high control or more realistic complex stimuli for external validity; some lack of realism may be desirable to refine experimental design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower realism for exploratory refinement and to obtain strong statistical relationships; reserve high-realism field testing for later validation of promising alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use response time as an unobtrusive measure of message favorability
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor subject response time (to very fine resolution) as rapidity of response appears related to message favorability (favorable messages processed most rapidly, neutral the slowest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider response latency as an additional unobtrusive metric of message valence; validate relationship in target contexts before relying on it for substantive inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for brand loyalty and personality as moderators of information processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that brand loyalty biases perception and selective processing of persuasive information, and personality variables (e.g., risk-taking propensity) influence how new information is processed and thereby affect choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brand loyalty and relevant personality measures as moderators or stratification variables in models of advertising effectiveness and information processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt messaging to organizational decision environment and perceived risk
rubrics_metrics.description: In organizational buying contexts, the decision environment (risk-averting vs risk-taking organizations) affects sensitivity to negative vs favorable information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor copy themes and persuasive messages to the decision maker's perceived environmental risk; negative information may be more influential in risk-averse settings while positive information may work better in risk-taking contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess empathic skills of advertising communicators (interpersonal and generalized-other sensitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate communicators on two types of empathic skills—(1) sensitivity to individual differences (interpersonal sensitivity) and (2) sensitivity to the generalized other (awareness of typical group responses)—which affect ability to judge self, others, what-to-say, and probable reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standardized tests (Type I tests for sensitivity to individuals, Type II for generalized-other) when studying or selecting professional communicators; hypothesis: professional advertising communicators will score higher on these empathic skills than the general population.
